```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r attach}
library(priogridR)
```

Cross-level analysis is not a single neutral operation. A population total
may be divided between overlapping regions, whereas a rate should normally be
averaged using the area represented by each source observation. The functions
in this vignette require that distinction to be stated explicitly.

## Grouped summaries

`pg_aggregate()` provides ordinary grouped summaries without introducing a
package-specific data class.

```{r aggregate}
cells <- data.frame(
  region = c("a", "a", "b"),
  events = c(1, 2, 4),
  population = c(100, 200, 150)
)

pg_aggregate(
  cells,
  values = c("events", "population"),
  by = "region",
  fun = "sum"
)
```

Weights may be supplied for means. Weighted totals are handled separately by
`pg_area_weight()` because they require a substantive allocation rule.

## Construct a spatial crosswalk

The target polygons are supplied by the researcher. This makes the source,
date, and territorial definition of administrative or country boundaries part
of the reproducible workflow.

```{r crosswalk}
config <- priogrid::pg_config(nrow = 18, ncol = 36, verbose = FALSE)

regions <- pg_geometry(342:344, config = config)
regions$region_id <- c("a", "a", "b")

crosswalk <- pg_crosswalk(
  regions,
  target_id = "region_id",
  pgid = 342:344,
  assignment = "fractional",
  config = config
)

crosswalk
```

Repeated target identifiers are dissolved before intersection. Fractional
assignment returns every positive-area overlap. `assignment = "largest"`
assigns the whole source cell to the target with its largest overlap, while
`assignment = "centroid"` uses the cell centre. Overlapping targets make a
centroid assignment ambiguous and therefore produce an error.

The returned diagnostics distinguish:

- `overlap_area_km2`: the observed geometric intersection;
- `allocation_area_km2`: the area used to weight intensive values;
- `cell_fraction`: the share of an extensive cell total assigned to a target;
- `target_fraction`: the share of the target represented by the intersection.

## Extensive and intensive variables

An extensive variable is additive over space. Population counts and event
counts are common examples. An intensive variable describes a local level or
rate and should not normally be summed.

```{r area-weight}
grid_data <- data.frame(
  pgid = 342:344,
  population = c(100, 200, 300),
  rate = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.4)
)

transferred <- pg_area_weight(
  grid_data,
  crosswalk,
  values = c("population", "rate"),
  target_id = "region_id",
  variable_type = c(
    population = "extensive",
    rate = "intensive"
  )
)

transferred
```

Each output variable receives a `_coverage` column. It is the share of the
relevant allocation weight represented by non-missing values. With
`na_rm = FALSE`, incomplete coverage produces a missing estimate but the
coverage diagnostic remains available.

## Aggregate to countries

`pg_to_country()` combines crosswalk construction and value transfer. It does
not download or bundle a particular country-boundary dataset.

```{r country}
country_result <- pg_to_country(
  grid_data,
  countries = regions,
  country_id = "region_id",
  values = "population",
  variable_type = "extensive",
  return_crosswalk = TRUE,
  config = config
)

country_result$data
```

Setting `return_crosswalk = TRUE` makes the exact spatial allocation available
for inspection, storage, and reuse.

One boundary definition is used in each call. When a historical panel spans
territorial changes, split it into documented boundary vintages, call
`pg_to_country()` separately for each vintage, and then combine the results.
This prevents the package from silently applying present-day borders to past
observations.

## Change grid resolution

Resolution changes use the same extensive-versus-intensive rules.

```{r resolution}
fine <- priogrid::pg_config(nrow = 18, ncol = 36, verbose = FALSE)
coarse <- priogrid::pg_config(nrow = 9, ncol = 18, verbose = FALSE)
fine_ids <- c(342L, 343L, 378L, 379L)
coordinates <- pg_coords_from_id(fine_ids, config = fine)

fine_data <- data.frame(
  pgid = fine_ids,
  population = rep(10, 4),
  rate = ifelse(coordinates$xcoord < 0, 2, 4)
)

coarse_data <- pg_change_resolution(
  fine_data,
  values = c("population", "rate"),
  from_config = fine,
  to_config = coarse,
  variable_type = c(
    population = "extensive",
    rate = "intensive"
  )
)

coarse_data
```

Extensive totals are fractionally allocated, so a complete transformation
preserves their global sum apart from numerical tolerance. Intensive values
are averaged with allocated area as the weight.

## Compare alternative representations

After two alternatives have been placed on the same grid,
`pg_compare_resolutions()` can return either row-level differences or compact
diagnostics.

```{r compare}
alternative <- coarse_data
alternative$rate <- alternative$rate + c(0.1, -0.1)

pg_compare_resolutions(
  coarse_data,
  alternative,
  values = c("population", "rate")
)

pg_compare_resolutions(
  coarse_data,
  alternative,
  values = "rate",
  detail = "cells"
)
```

The summary reports matching coverage, mean difference, mean absolute
difference, root mean squared error, and correlation. These diagnostics do not
decide which spatial representation is substantively preferable; they expose
the consequences of that choice.
